findings.issue: The leading-dash guard tests the RAW param (`params.branch?.startsWith('-')`) while lines 101, 125 and 143 use the TRIMMED value (`params.branch?.trim()`). A branch of `' -f'` passes the guard, is trimmed to `-f`, `findByBranch(envelope, '-f')` returns undefined so `target` is undefined, the self-removal guard at line 148 cannot fire, and the tool runs `wt remove -f --foreground`. Per .pi/sdd/git-workspace-extension/discovery.md:46, `wt remove` with no branch argument defaults to the current worktree, so that argv force-removes the worktree the session is running in and deletes its branch. Reproduced end to end against a PATH `wt` stub: branch `' -f'` produced calls `list --format=json`, `remove -f --foreground`, `list --format=json` and the result "Removed the worktree for -f.". The same ordering hole applies to `create` and `switch`, where the trimmed branch lands in `wt switch` argv as a bare positional. Impact is bounded by the confirm dialog rendering the raw string and by git rejecting such branch names later, but the guard added in this diff exists precisely to make this unreachable and it is one character away.
findings.fix: Trim once before the guard and reuse the trimmed value: `const branch = params.branch?.trim(); if (branch?.startsWith('-')) return text('worktree branch must not start with "-".')` at the top of `execute`, then use `branch` in the create/switch/remove cases (remove still falls back to `findCurrent(...)`). Add a test mirroring tests/git-worktree.test.ts:126 with `branch: ' -f'` asserting `/must not start with/` and `wt.callArgs()` equal to `[]`.

findings.issue: `parseEnvelope` reads `schema` into the model and nothing ever checks it. If a future Worktrunk bumps the JSON schema and moves or renames `items[].worktree`, `list` silently answers "No worktrees found." and `status` answers "No current worktree found" instead of the "could not parse" error the spec promises for unexpected wt output, so the agent is told there are no worktrees when there are.
findings.fix: No linter enforces this. Either reject a present-but-unknown schema in `parseEnvelope` (return undefined when `typeof data.schema === 'number' && data.schema !== 2`) so the existing "could not parse" path fires, or drop the unused `schema` field and note that the tool keys off the documented schema-2 shape.

findings.issue: The `branch` description promises "remove defaults to the current worktree", but that default can never succeed: `loadWorktrees` runs `wt list` with `cwd: ctx.cwd`, so the item with `worktree.current == true` (discovery.md:53,55) is always the worktree containing the session cwd, and the `ownsCwd` realpath guard refuses it every time. The model reads this description, so it will try `remove` with no branch and get "Refusing to remove ...: it is the worktree this session is running in." The real rule is only stated in the promptGuidelines.
findings.fix: No linter enforces this. Drop the clause and describe the parameter as "Branch to create, remove or switch to (required for remove)", or state the default and its refusal: "remove defaults to the current worktree and is then refused, so pass a branch".

findings.issue: `resolveBase` falls back only to `refs/remotes/origin/<candidate>`, so a repo whose only remote is named `upstream` (the normal shape for a fork) and whose local `main`/`master` is gone fails with "Could not find base branch (main or master) as a local or origin ref" even though `upstream/main` exists. Recoverable via the `base` param, but the error names a remote the user may not have.
findings.fix: No linter enforces this. List remotes with `git remote` (or `gh repo view`) and probe the first/only remote, or name the remote actually searched in the error text.

findings.issue: The ExtensionContext factory is copy-pasted in all three new test files (tests/git-worktree.test.ts:34, tests/git-gh.test.ts:48 and :56 `readOnlyCtx`, tests/git-commit.test.ts:25), each a slightly different variant of the same `asMock` block. A change to the ctx shape or the confirm signature has to be made in three places.
findings.fix: No linter enforces this (the duplication is across files, not statements). Move one `toolCtx(cwd, { confirm })` helper next to `loadRegisteredTool` in tests/helpers.ts and have the three files call it.

findings.issue: `mise run check` runs `test` (all 20 files) and then `coverage` (the same 4 files again with `--coverage`), so the git-tool tests execute twice per gate; measured at 7.65s + 6.33s locally.
findings.fix: No linter or formatter rule covers task composition. Either give `test` `--coverage` with the thresholds and drop the separate task, or narrow `coverage` to the new modules only.

findings.issue: The `branch.<branch>.pushRemote` / `remote.pushDefault` config resolution never executes in any test. The v8 coverage report shows statements 103 (`remote = config.stdout.trim()`) and 104 (`break`) at zero count, and the guard `if (config.ok && config.stdout.trim())` on line 102 has branch counts `[0, 12]` - the true side is never taken. Every test repo either has an upstream set (so the loop is skipped) or no such config (so `git config` returns empty and the falsy side is taken). This is the code that picks the push destination, the one decision in the tool that writes to a remote the user did not name explicitly, and it has zero execution history. I confirmed the behaviour is correct by driving it manually, but a regression that swapped the two config keys, dropped the `break`, or ignored `config.ok` would leave the suite green.
findings.fix: Add a tool-level test on a repo with two remotes (`fork`, `upstream`), no upstream on the branch, and `branch.feature.pushRemote` set to `upstream`. Assert the exact push argv is `['push','--set-upstream','upstream','feature']` and that no push reached `fork` (e.g. `git branch --format=%(refname)` on each bare remote). A second case with only `remote.pushDefault` set and no `pushRemote` pins the loop order.

findings.issue: The 'Multiple git remotes ... with no upstream' refusal never executes. Statement 112 (the message template literal) has zero count and the `if` on line 110 has branch counts `[0, 10]`. This is the guard that stops the tool from guessing a remote, and it is the one case in the resolution ladder with no test: `No git remote is configured` is covered (tests/git-commit.test.ts:299), `prefers origin over the first remote` is covered (tests/git-commit.test.ts:449), and the upstream case is covered, but a repo with two non-origin remotes and no upstream config falls straight through every existing test. If the `remotes.length > 1` condition were changed to `>= 1` or deleted, no test would fail and the tool would push to a guessed remote.
findings.fix: Add a test on a real repo with two bare remotes named `fork` and `upstream`, no upstream on the branch and no `pushRemote`/`pushDefault`, then `{ message, push: true }` with a confirm spy. Assert the result matches `/Multiple git remotes \(fork, upstream\)/`, that `prompted` is `false`, and that `git rev-parse --verify origin/feature` and `upstream/feature` both still throw (nothing was pushed anywhere).

findings.issue: The message-mode staged-diff failure is untested. Statement 55 (`if (!staged.ok) return text(staged.error)`) has zero count in the coverage report. The parallel no-message-mode path is covered by tests/git-commit.test.ts:395 (non-repo cwd), but the message path runs `git diff --cached --name-only` and its two error strings (`git (not found on PATH)` at index.ts:21 and the exit-code dump at :25) are never rendered through the commit tool. A regression that, say, dropped the `!staged.ok` check would let a failed diff fall through to `git commit` and produce a confusing empty-index message.
findings.fix: Add one test driving `{ message: 'feat: add b' }` with `ctx` pointing at a directory that is not a git repo, asserting the result matches `/^git diff --cached --name-only --no-ext-diff failed with exit code 129/` and that the exit-129 usage dump is capped at 20 lines. A second case with `restrictPath(emptyPathDir())` pins the `git (not found on PATH)` text on this path.

findings.issue: Three untested guard paths on the worktree tool, all zero-count in the v8 report: statement 104 (`create`'s pre-check `if (!loaded.ok) return text(loaded.error)`), statement 108 (`create`'s `wt switch` missing-binary branch), and statement 94 (`status`'s `if (!loaded.ok)`). The twins for `remove` exist (tests/git-worktree.test.ts:118 covers `switch`'s missing binary, :124 covers `remove`'s self-deleting stub, :144 covers `remove`'s failing pre-check list), and the test at :124 already contains the exact "stub deletes itself after serving `list`" trick needed for the `create` case, so the gap is an oversight rather than a limitation. The `create` pre-check is the guard that stops a removal-free mutation on stale state, so it matters more than its `list` twin.
findings.fix: Reuse the self-deleting stub pattern from tests/git-worktree.test.ts:124 for `create`: a `wt` that serves a valid `list` envelope then removes itself, then call `{ operation: 'create', branch: 'new-thing' }` and assert the result matches `/wt \(not found on PATH\)/`. Add a `create` case with `stubOnPath('wt', 'exit 4')` asserting `/wt list failed with exit code 4/` and that no `switch` argv was recorded. Add a `status` case with the same failing-list stub.

findings.issue: Four zero-count error paths on the gh tool: statement 88 (`auth`'s `json.missing` branch on the `--json hosts` call), statement 94 (`auth`'s `human.missing` branch on the fallback form), statement 103 (`repo view`'s `ghFailure`), and statement 159 (`ghFailure('gh pr create', result)` - gh exits non-zero printing no PR URL). The `pr view` and `pr checks` twins of the missing-binary path are covered (tests/git-gh.test.ts:501, :562) and the non-zero-with-URL `pr create` case is covered (:427), so the plain-failure `pr create` case and both `auth` branches are holes in an otherwise complete matrix. The round-1 review already flagged the `auth` missing-binary branches; they are still open.
findings.fix: Three tests. (a) `{ operation: 'auth' }` under `restrictPath(emptyPathDir())` asserting the `gh auth status` `ghFailure` text. (b) `{ operation: 'repo view' }` with `stubGh('printf "boom\\n" >&2\nexit 1')` asserting `/gh repo view failed with exit code 1/` and that `boom` appears. (c) A `pr create` test using the real-repo base resolution with `stubGh('printf "validation failed\\n" >&2\nexit 1')` and a confirm that returns true, asserting the `ghFailure` text and, since the declined variant already proves gating, that the confirm was actually reached.

findings.issue: Six defensive parse/format fallbacks are zero-count: `prChecksArgs` with a `target` (ghops.ts:95 - no test calls it with a target), `parseAuthHosts` skipping a non-array `accounts` (:245) and a non-record account entry (:250), `formatPrView`'s `isDraft` flag (:178), `parseRepoView`'s non-record `defaultBranchRef` (:267), and `parseItem` with a non-string `branch` (worktrees.ts:71). Each is a malformed-input guard on a pure function, so a unit test is cheap. `parseAuthHosts` at :250 was flagged in the round-1 review and is still open.
findings.fix: Extend the existing table-driven parse tests. For `parseAuthHosts`, feed `{"hosts":{"github.com":["x",{"login":"a"}]}}` and assert the exact emitted lines (`'x'` skipped). For the rest, one case each in the existing `formatPrView, summarizeChecks and formatRepoView cover their fallbacks` and `parseAuthHosts handles the hosts envelope and rejects junk` tests.

findings.issue: The per-file line threshold of 95 is met by git-commit/index.ts with only 95.58% (a 0.58pp margin, roughly one statement). That file is also the least-covered of the seven at 81.65% branches, so it is the file most likely to need the next edit. A single added uncovered line anywhere in it turns CI red for a change that is otherwise fine, which trains people to raise the threshold instead of adding the test.
findings.fix: Either lower the per-file line threshold to 92 (still far above the 80% floor and above every other file here) so the gate catches a real regression rather than a single line, or close the six zero-count statements in the findings above, which lifts the file to ~99% and restores headroom.

findings.issue: The acceptance criterion 'Nothing under `agent/` is written at runtime by these tools' is still verified only by a manual `rg` for `writeFileSync`/`mkdirSync`, as the plan itself states. I confirmed the grep is clean today, but nothing in the suite or in oxlint enforces it, so a future edit that adds a state file under `agent/` passes every gate until `mise run drift` catches it at runtime. This was a round-1 nit and is still open.
findings.fix: Add an oxlint `no-restricted-imports` or `no-restricted-syntax` rule banning `node:fs` write calls under `agent/extensions/**`, or a vitest test that walks the extension dirs and fails on `writeFileSync`/`mkdirSync`/`appendFile`/`rmSync`. Either turns a review checklist item into a build failure.

findings.issue: "// Oldest commit ahead of the base, matching `gh pr create --fill`." A justification for our own line (`commits.at(-1)?.subject` at :147) that is also factually wrong. Evidence: gh's own `initDefaultTitleBody` (cli/cli trunk, pkg/cmd/pr/create/create.go) does `if len(commits) == 1 || useFirstCommit { state.Title = commits[len(commits)-1].Title } else { state.Title = humanize(headRef) }`, and `useFirstCommit` is `opts.FillFirst`. So plain `--fill` takes `commits[len-1]` only for a single-commit branch; with more than one commit it titles the PR after the humanized branch name. The oldest-commit title is `--fill-first`, a separate flag (verified on the local `gh 2.101.0`: `-f, --fill  Use commit info for title and body` alongside `--fill-first  Use first commit info for title and body`). The path here handles up to 50 commits (`gitLogArgs`), and tests/git-gh.test.ts:344 drives it with three commits and asserts the oldest subject 'add b', so the claim is wrong exactly where the code runs. The "oldest" half is also derivable: `gitLogArgs` is a plain `git log` (newest-first) and `parseCommits` preserves that order, so `.at(-1)` is the oldest by construction.
findings.fix: delete. The behavior is a design choice, not a constraint, so it clears no keep-list item. If the oldest-commit title must stay, the intent belongs in the code shape (e.g. a named local like `const oldestSubject = commits.at(-1)?.subject` in `pr create`, `git-gh/index.ts:147`), not in a claim about a gh flag that does not behave this way.

findings.issue: "// Match git's own default: prefer origin, then a single configured remote." Restates the two lines below it and gets git's order backwards. git's `remotes_remote_for_branch` (git/remote.c:673-687) is: branch.pushremote, then remote.pushDefault, then, only if `remotes_nr == 1`, that single remote, else the literal "origin". The two orders agree in practice, so the comment's claim is not a documented surprise we are stuck with; it is our own ordering choice. Keep-list item 2 is a plausible cover, hence nits rather than mustKill.
findings.fix: delete. Refactor target: the inline block at git-commit/index.ts:99-110. Extract it as `resolvePushRemote(branch, upstream, remotes)` in git-gh-style pure form; the function name plus the ordered returns carry the intent, and the git-compatible order becomes checkable in one place.

findings.issue: "/** True when the process could not be spawned, for example when the binary is absent from PATH. */" Longer than the contract it carries. The field name says it, all three callers render `missing` as "(not found on PATH)", and the "for example" is loose: the only spawn error that sets the flag is `error.code === 'ENOENT'` (exec.ts:69), so a non-ENOENT spawn failure would report `missing: false`. Keep-list item 4 plausibly covers a cross-module contract, hence nits rather than mustKill.
findings.fix: delete. If the ENOENT-only contract must be pinned, the code shape does it: derive the flag once, e.g. `const missing = code === 'ENOENT'` with `code` narrowed to a `NodeJS.ErrnoException`, so the field carries no wider promise than the implementation.

findings.issue: `const branch = requestedBranch || findCurrent(loaded.envelope)?.branch` falls back to a display placeholder. `findCurrent` returns `summarize(item)`, which substitutes the literal string `'(detached)'` when the item has no string `branch` (worktrees.ts:113), and that string is then pushed as the branch positional: `wt remove (detached) [--foreground]`. The user sees `Remove (detached)?` in the dialog and then a wt error naming a branch that does not exist. The fallback also cannot do anything useful in the normal case: when the current worktree is attached, `target` resolves to the current worktree, `ownsCwd` fires at line 147 and the call is refused, so `remove` with no branch either refuses or runs a bogus command. The parameter is already documented as `(required for remove)` at index.ts:26, so the fallback contradicts the contract it is supposed to serve. I could not observe a detached `wt list` envelope on this machine (creating one is not a read-only action), so the `'(detached)'` arm is inferred from the code and from .pi/sdd/git-workspace-extension/discovery.md:27, which shows `worktree.detached` as a separate flag; if wt instead emits `"branch": ""` the observable symptom is the misleading `remove needs a branch when there is no current worktree` text instead. Either way the path is wrong.
findings.fix: Delete the fallback and require the branch: `const branch = requestedBranch; if (!branch) return text('worktree remove requires a branch name (the current worktree is never removable from inside it).')`. That also removes the only path by which the `realPath(cwd)`-based guard can be evaluated against a non-current target, and the guard's best-effort behaviour (it degrades to a raw-path compare when `realpathSync(cwd)` throws) stops mattering for the no-argument form. If the fallback is kept, read the branch from the raw item rather than the summary and return a dedicated message when it is missing or equals the placeholder. Add a test: `stubList({schema:2,items:[{worktree:{path:'/wt/x',current:true}}]})` with `{operation:'remove'}` asserting `/requires a branch/` and that `wt.callArgs()` has no `remove` entry.

findings.issue: `run` spawns `git`, `gh` and `wt` with `maxBuffer` but no `timeout`, and `RunOptions` exposes only `cwd` and `signal`. A child that never exits leaves the returned promise pending forever, so the tool call never returns and the agent turn hangs until the user presses escape (pi aborts via the gate signal, which is the only escape hatch). The concrete hang is `git push` over ssh: `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` and `GH_PROMPT_DISABLED=1` stop git and gh prompts, but neither stops `ssh` from opening /dev/tty for a passphrase on an encrypted key, and a black-holed TCP connect from `gh` has no bound either. pi's own bash tool bounds this with `timeoutMs` (default 120000 in chunk-4DKZACXI.js), so the repo already has the precedent this helper drops. A killed child is also reported opaquely: for any failure that wrote nothing and is neither ENOENT nor a maxBuffer overrun, `stderrText` at line 75 is `err || (aborted ? error.message : '')`, which is `''`, so the worktree and commit callers render `wt list failed with exit code 1: ` / `git commit failed with exit code 1: ` with a dangling colon and no explanation (only git-gh has the `'(no output from gh)'` placeholder).
findings.fix: Add `timeoutMs?: number` to `RunOptions`, pass it through as `execOptions.timeout` (Node's `execFile` kills the child and returns), default it to something like 120_000 for every call, and treat the kill as a failure: when `error.killed` is set, return `stderr: command + ' timed out after ' + timeoutMs + 'ms'`. Also give the empty-detail case a placeholder in `agent/extensions/git-worktree/index.ts:51,110,130,173` and `agent/extensions/git-commit/index.ts:25,63,137` so a silent failure never renders as a colon with nothing after it. One test: `run(process.execPath, ['-e', 'setTimeout(()=>{}, 60000)'], { timeoutMs: 50 })` asserting `ok === false` and stderr mentioning the timeout.

findings.issue: `resolveBase` now probes every remote from `git remote` (index.ts:49-56, 60-64) instead of only `origin`, but the refusal it feeds still says `as a local or origin ref`. A user whose only remote is `upstream` reads an error naming a remote that was never searched, which sends them down the wrong path. The test at tests/git-gh.test.ts:303 only matches `/Could not find base branch/` so it does not pin the stale half.
findings.fix: No linter or formatter rule covers message text. Change the string to `Could not find base branch ${looked} as a local ref or refs/remotes/<remote>/<name> for any configured remote.` and tighten tests/git-gh.test.ts:303 to assert the full sentence.

findings.issue: `stubOnPath` records argv as fields joined by `\x1e` and `readCallArgs` splits records on the same byte. One argument the tools actually pass contains that byte: `gitLogArgs` in agent/extensions/git-gh/ghops.ts:114 is `['log','-n','50','--format=%s%n%b\x1e', ...]`. Any current or future assertion on a stubbed `git log` call therefore reads `--format=%s%n%b` and `main..HEAD` as two separate arguments. Nothing breaks today only because the gh tests stub `git` and then assert on the `gh` stub's log, never on the git stub's.
findings.fix: No linter covers the fixture encoding. Make each field unambiguous before writing, e.g. base64-encode every argument in the printf (`printf '%s\0' "$@" | base64`) and decode in `readCallArgs`, or switch the field separator to a byte git never emits in an argument and keep the NUL record separator as-is.

findings.issue: `mise run check` runs `{ task = "test" }` (mise.toml:25, all 21 files) and then `{ task = "coverage" }` (mise.toml:30, the same 4 git-tool files again). Measured here: 9.05s for the full run and 8.45s for the coverage run, so the four new test files execute twice per gate.
findings.fix: No linter or formatter rule covers task composition. Give `tasks.test` the `--coverage` flag so vitest.config.ts thresholds apply to the whole suite, and drop `tasks.coverage` from the `check` list, or narrow `tasks.coverage` to `--coverage.reporter=text --coverage.thresholds.lines=0`-style no-op and keep it as a separate manual task.

findings.issue: The plan describes a helper that does not exist: line 34 and task 1 at line 51 both promise `agent/extensions/lib/exec.ts` exporting `run` and `tryRun`, and line 27 documents the signature as `run(cmd, args, { cwd, signal, env })`. The shipped module exports only `run`, takes `{ cwd, signal }`, and hardcodes the non-interactive env internally, so there is no `tryRun` and no `env` override. The plan is the artifact the next implementer reads.
findings.fix: No linter covers prose. Update plan.md:34 and :51 to the shipped `run` signature and drop `tryRun`, or add the `tryRun` wrapper if a later change needs it.

findings.issue: The last rung of the push-remote ladder, `if (!remote && remotes.length === 1) remote = remotes[0] ?? ''`, never executes. v8 shows statement 110 at count 0 and the `if` with branch counts [0, 13]. Every push test repo has either zero remotes (git-commit.test.ts:387), two remotes including origin (:537, :325, :338, :350) or an upstream, so the true side is never taken. This is the ordinary fork-clone shape: one remote named `upstream`, a fresh branch, `push: true`, no push config. I drove it manually (temp repo, bare remote named `upstream`, no upstream tracking, no pushRemote/pushDefault): the tool returned `Committed and pushed feature to upstream:` and the bare remote gained `refs/heads/feature`, so the behaviour is correct and this is a coverage gap, not a bug. But a regression that dropped this rung (falling through to `No git remote is configured`) or reordered it above the pushRemote loop would leave the suite fully green, because every existing multi-remote test has two or more remotes and therefore never depends on the single-remote rung.
findings.fix: Add a tool-level test: build a temp repo whose only remote is a bare repo named `upstream`, no `branch.feature.pushRemote` and no `remote.pushDefault`, stage a change, `{ message, push: true }` with a confirm spy returning true. Assert the exact push argv `['push', '--set-upstream', 'upstream', 'feature']`, that the confirm body named `upstream/feature`, and that `git branch --format=%(refname)` in the bare repo contains `refs/heads/feature`. Reuse the `repoWithRemote` + `stubGit()` pattern from git-commit.test.ts:325.

findings.issue: `pr update` with no `target` never runs. Both cond-exprs on 180-181 report counts [4, 0]: all four tool-level `pr update` calls (tests/git-gh.test.ts:216, :231, :243, :256, :490, :494) pass `target: '12'`, so `watched` is always `Pull request: 12` and the `Pull request: current branch` arm is dead in the suite. `target` is declared optional (index.ts:34) and the tool's own promptGuidelines do not require it, so this is the common "rename the PR for the branch I am on" call. I drove it against a stub gh: the confirm body was `Pull request: current branch\nTitle: x` and gh received `pr edit --title x` with no positional. The behaviour is correct, but the only thing telling the user which PR a mutating, confirm-gated call will rewrite is that ternary, and inverting it (or dropping the `target ?` arm so it always says `?`) would not fail a single test. The argv builder itself is unit-tested for the no-target case (git-gh.test.ts:797), which is exactly why the tool-level path can regress unnoticed.
findings.fix: Add one test calling `{ operation: 'pr update', title: 'x' }` with no target and a confirm spy that captures the dialog body; assert the body contains `Pull request: current branch`, that `gh.callArgs()` equals `[['pr','edit','--title','x']]`, and that the result reports the URL. Add the declined variant asserting `gh.calls()` is empty, mirroring the existing declined tests.

findings.issue: Still open from the previous two rounds: the `auth` human-form missing-binary guard, `if (human.missing) return text(ghFailure('gh auth status', human))`, has branch counts [0, 2] and is the only statement in git-gh/index.ts with zero count. The `restrictPath(emptyPathDir())` test at git-gh.test.ts:385 covers the first call's guard (now line 98), not this one. Reaching it needs gh to disappear between the two spawns, so it is defensive rather than a production path, and the rendering it produces is identical to the covered line 98. The self-deleting stub pattern already exists at tests/git-worktree.test.ts:124, so the test is cheap if the branch is worth pinning.
findings.fix: Either add a `gh` stub that serves the `--json hosts` call and then removes itself, then assert `{ operation: 'auth' }` matches /gh \(not found on PATH\)/; or, if the branch is judged unreachable, return the guard's error from the first missing check and delete line 104 so there is nothing left uncovered.

findings.issue: `if (json.ok)` has counts [3, 0]: no test makes `gh auth status --json hosts` exit non-zero, so the fall-through to the human form after a failing JSON call is unexercised. I checked the real binary: gh 2.101.0 with an empty config dir exits 0 and prints `{"hosts":{}}` when logged out, which is what the logged-out test at git-gh.test.ts:187 stubs, so this arm only fires on an older or different gh. I drove it with a stub that exits 3 on the JSON form and the tool correctly returned the human-form message, so the behaviour is right; the gap is that a change which returned early on `!json.ok` instead of falling through would not fail any test.
findings.fix: Add one case to the auth test: a `gh` stub that exits non-zero for `--json hosts` and prints to stderr for the plain form, asserting the result is the human-form stderr and that both `auth status` invocations were recorded.

findings.issue: `params.base ? `"${params.base}"` : '(main or master)'` reports [0, 1]: the only test that hits the unresolvable-base error (git-gh.test.ts:292) omits `base`, so the message never names the base the caller actually asked for. I confirmed the untested arm is correct: `{ operation: 'pr create', base: 'nope' }` returns `Could not find base branch "nope" as a local or origin ref.`. A regression that always printed `(main or main or master)` would leave the suite green on a user-facing error path.
findings.fix: Add a case alongside :292 calling `{ operation: 'pr create', base: 'nope' }` in a repo with no such ref, asserting the result contains `"nope"` and that the confirm was never reached.

findings.issue: `pr create` when gh exits 0 but prints no PR URL is untested: the cond-expr on 167 is [6, 0] and the `result.stdout.trim() || 'Pull request created.'` chain is [0, 0], so neither the echo-stdout arm nor the `Pull request created.` placeholder has run. The declined variant (:476), the non-zero-with-URL variant (:460) and the non-zero-without-URL variant (:404) are all covered, so this is the last cell of the `pr create` result matrix. I drove it with a stub that exits 0 silently and got `Pull request created.`, so the behaviour is correct.
findings.fix: Add a `pr create` case with `stubGh('exit 0')` and a confirm returning true, asserting the result is exactly `Pull request created.`, plus a variant that prints a non-URL line to stdout and asserts that line is returned instead.

findings.issue: The malformed-JSON-object guards in the pure parsers are still zero-count: `parseAuthHosts`'s `!isRecord(data) || !isRecord(data.hosts)` on 245 ([0, 7]) and `parseRepoView`'s `!isRecord(data)` on 267 ([0, 5]). The malformed-shape test at git-gh.test.ts:773 feeds input that fails `JSON.parse`, so it returns at the catch above and never reaches these lines. Also still open from the previous round: the non-array `accounts` and non-record account-entry skips on 248/250, and one arm of the `?? '?'` pair on 182. These are cheap unit cases on pure functions, and they are the difference between the tool saying "output this tool could not parse" and rendering `undefined` into the result.
findings.fix: Extend the existing table-driven parse tests: feed `{"hosts":{"github.com":["x",{"login":"a"}],"gitlab.com":{}}}` to `parseAuthHosts` and assert the exact emitted lines; feed `[]` and `{"hosts":"nope"}` and assert `undefined`; feed `[]` to `parseRepoView` and assert `undefined`; add a `ParsePrView` with one of `headRefName`/`baseRefName` missing and assert the `?` placeholder.

findings.issue: Three untested degrade-to-less-information arms on the destructive path: `target ? realPath(target.path) : ''` on 145 ([10, 0]), `selected ? ... : 'Switched to branch ...'` on 136 ([1, 0]) and `target ? ... : branch` on 159 ([7, 0]). The case behind all three is `remove` (or `switch`) naming a branch that is not in the `wt list` envelope, e.g. a typo or a branch wt has not created. Then `ownsCwd` is false, the confirm body degrades to the bare branch name with no path and no dirty-state summary, and `wt remove <name>` runs anyway. The existing remove tests (git-worktree.test.ts:292, :308, :325, :356, :366, :381, :398) all name a branch that is in the envelope. The behaviour is not unsafe here, since wt refuses to remove a worktree it does not know, but the confirm text is the only description of what is about to be deleted.
findings.fix: Add a `remove` case with a stub envelope containing one worktree and `{ operation: 'remove', branch: 'typo' }`: assert the confirm body contains `Remove typo?`, that the recorded `wt` argv is `['remove','typo','--foreground']`, and pin what the tool returns when wt then reports failure. Add a `switch` case where the follow-up list no longer contains the branch, asserting the `Switched to branch X.` fallback.

findings.issue: The plan's acceptance criterion is "nothing under `agent/` is written at runtime by these tools", but the guard is a source-text regex over `agent/extensions/{git-commit,git-gh,git-worktree}` only, and only for `writeFileSync|appendFileSync|mkdirSync|rmSync|writeFile|mkdir`. It does not scan `agent/extensions/lib/exec.ts`, which is where a write helper would most plausibly be added, and it does not match `node:fs/promises`, `createWriteStream`, `copyFile`, `rename`, `truncate`, `unlink` or `rmdir`, so several ways of writing state pass it. It is also a test of source text rather than behaviour, so it proves the string is absent, not that nothing is written. The test is still a real improvement on the previous manual `rg`, and `mise run drift` catches modifications to already-tracked files, so this is a nit rather than a gap.
findings.fix: Either widen the scan to all of `agent/extensions/**` and add the remaining fs write APIs to the pattern, or replace it with a behavioural test that runs each tool against a temp repo and asserts the extension tree's mtimes and file list are unchanged. If the text scan stays, add an oxlint `no-restricted-syntax` rule over `agent/extensions/**` so the check is a build failure rather than a regex in a test.

findings.issue: The `stderr.trim() || stdout.trim() || '(no output)'` chain is copy-pasted into eight error strings across the three tools (git-commit 25, 63, 137; git-gh 107, 154; git-worktree 51, 110, 130, 173) and in every instance only the first arm is ever exercised. Coverage shows the remaining arms at zero: git-commit 25 [3,0,0], 63 [1,0,0], 137 [1,0,0]; git-gh 107 [1,0,0], 154 [1,0]; git-worktree 51 [7,0], 110 [1,0], 130 [1,0], 173 [1,0]. The visible consequence is that a tool failure whose diagnostics land on stdout instead of stderr renders as `failed with exit code 1: ` with nothing after the colon, and a silent failure never reaches the `'(no output)'` placeholder. One test against a stub that writes to stdout and one against a silent stub would cover the pattern once per tool.
findings.fix: Extract a single `detailOf(result)` helper next to `truncateOutput` in agent/extensions/lib/exec.ts that returns `stderr.trim() || stdout.trim() || '(no output)'`, use it at all eight sites, and add two cases in tests/exec.test.ts plus one tool-level test per tool that fails with output on stdout only and one that fails silently.

findings.issue: "// Prefer origin, then a single configured remote." Pure narration of the two lines below it (`if (!remote && remotes.includes('origin')) remote = 'origin'` then `if (!remote && remotes.length === 1) remote = remotes[0] ?? ''`). The ordering is legible directly from those two conditionals, the preceding config loop already spells its own priority in the `['branch.${branch}.pushRemote', 'remote.pushDefault']` key list, and nothing here is forced by a dependency: it is our own fallback policy. `git blame -L 106,110` shows the comment landed in f8934a8 on top of code already written in cc70f94, i.e. it explains code that was already self-explanatory. No keep-list clause applies.
findings.fix: delete. No refactor needed; the two conditionals are the spec. If the author still wants the ordering legible, the smallest reshape is to build an ordered candidate list (`[upstreamRemote, pushRemote, pushDefault, ...(remotes.includes('origin') ? ['origin'] : []), ...(remotes.length === 1 ? remotes : [])]`) and take the first non-empty entry, which makes the priority the data rather than a prose note.

findings.issue: "Run a command with an argument array and never throw on a non-zero exit. Failures are returned as `{ ok: false }` with the command's stderr so tools can surface them as text instead of exceptions." The never-throw-on-non-zero clause is a real contract the three calling extensions rely on and is not derivable from the `Promise<RunResult>` signature, so keep-list item 4 plausibly covers the middle of this block. But it is longer than the contract needs: "Run a command with an argument array" restates `run(command: string, args: string[])` verbatim, and "so tools can surface them as text instead of exceptions" is rationale for a return type the signature already declares. Borderline keep rather than a clean one.
findings.fix: delete the opening restatement and the trailing rationale, keeping only the never-throw guarantee if the contract is worth stating at the boundary.

findings.issue: "// Real `wt list --format=json` (schema 2) change flags are booleans with a diff count object." Asserts that the CLEAN_CHANGES/DIRTY_CHANGES fixtures right below mirror the real vendor wire format rather than being invented, which is a claim about an external tool's output that a reader cannot check from the literal alone (a fixture is by definition a guess). Keep-list item 2 plausibly covers it and the claim is accurate per .pi/sdd/git-workspace-extension/discovery.md:22,27, so it is a borderline keep, not a clear kill. It is also the only place recording that `boolean` (not `number`) is the form real wt emits, which is why `WtChanges` has to tolerate both.
findings.fix: keep only if the boolean-vs-number point is wanted; the '(schema 2)' parenthetical and 'change flags are' phrasing both restate the literal below. A narrower justification would earn the keep outright.

findings.issue: `timeoutMs` is exported and unit-tested but no call site ever passes it, so the 120s default applies identically to `wt list` and to `git push` (agent/extensions/git-commit/index.ts:130). A first push of a large branch over a slow link is killed at 120s and the user gets `git push failed with exit code 1: git timed out after 120000ms` with the commit left local. The kill itself is safe (git only updates the remote ref at the end), but for a local/path remote a killed `git push` can leave a stale pack temp or ref lock in the receiving repo, and the tool offers no way to give the one call that needs a longer bound a longer bound.
findings.fix: Pass a larger bound at the push call site, e.g. `run('git', pushArgs, { cwd, signal, timeoutMs: 600_000 })`, and keep 120_000 as the default for the read-only calls. No linter enforces this; the fix is the `timeoutMs` field that already exists on RunOptions.

findings.issue: `ghFailure` re-implements the detail chain that `detailOf` (agent/extensions/lib/exec.ts:27) now owns, with a different placeholder ('(no output from gh)' vs '(no output)'), and the `git log` failure at index.ts:154 uses a third hand-rolled chain with no placeholder at all, so a silent `git log` failure renders `git log failed with exit code 1: ` with a dangling colon. The three tools now disagree on what an empty failure looks like.
findings.fix: No linter covers this. Use `detailOf(result)` at index.ts:69 and index.ts:154, or give `ghFailure` an explicit `empty` parameter so the one intentional difference (naming gh) is declared rather than duplicated. Add a case in tests/git-gh.test.ts driving a `git log` stub that exits non-zero silently and assert the result contains '(no output)'.

findings.issue: The remove arm calls `loadWorktrees` (a `wt list` spawn) before checking `if (!branch)`, so every `remove` with no branch pays a child process for a call that is guaranteed to be rejected three lines later. tests/git-worktree.test.ts pins the wasted call by asserting `wt.callArgs()` equals `[['list','--format=json']]` for the no-branch case, so the ordering is now the tested contract.
findings.fix: No linter enforces this. Move the `if (!branch) return text(...)` check above `const loaded = await loadWorktrees(...)` and change that test to assert `wt.callArgs()).toEqual([])`.

findings.issue: The push destination is derived by slicing `@{upstream}` at the first slash: `upstreamRemote = 'my'`, `upstreamRef = 'remote/main'` for an upstream string of `my/remote/main`. Git stores remote names as config section names, which may contain '/', so a remote named e.g. `company/prod` makes the tool push to a remote named `company` that does not exist. I could not create a repo to confirm the exact git behaviour here (read-only review), so treat the trigger as unconfirmed; the slicing itself is unambiguously ambiguous, and the same `indexOf('/')` heuristic also treats a local-tracking upstream (which has no slash) as no upstream. It fails safe: the push errors and the commit stays local.
findings.fix: Read the keys git itself uses instead of parsing the display string: `git config branch.<branch>.remote` for the remote and `git config branch.<branch>.merge` (`refs/heads/<name>`) for the ref. That also removes the `hasUpstream` slash heuristic. If the config lookup is added, cover it with a test repo whose remote name contains a slash.

findings.issue: The push-remote resolution ladder (upstream remote, then the `branch.*.pushRemote` / `remote.pushDefault` config loop, then origin, then the single-remote case, then two refusals) is roughly 30 lines inline in `execute`, which is now over 100 lines mixing staging, committing, branch discovery, remote resolution, confirm and push. The two sibling extensions keep this logic in a pure module (`worktrees.ts`, `ghops.ts`, `message.ts`) so it can be unit tested without PATH stubs; this ladder instead needs five live git repos in the test file. The extra blank line before the two `if (!remote ...)` rungs (105-108) is a symptom of the inline shape.
findings.fix: No linter enforces this. Extract `resolvePushRemote({ branch, upstreamRemote, remotes, configFor })` as a pure function in a new `agent/extensions/git-commit/push.ts` (or in message.ts) returning a discriminated result, keep the two refusals in index.ts, and build the priority as data: `[upstreamRemote, ...(remotes.includes('origin') ? ['origin'] : []), ...(remotes.length === 1 ? remotes : [])]`. That makes the ordering testable without git and removes the need for a comment to explain it.

findings.issue: `mise run check` runs `{ task = "test" }` (all 21 files) and then `{ task = "coverage" }`, which re-runs tests/exec.test.ts, tests/git-commit.test.ts, tests/git-gh.test.ts and tests/git-worktree.test.ts a second time. Measured here: 12.5s for the full run plus the coverage run, so the four heaviest files execute twice per gate. This is the same finding as the previous two rounds and it is still open.
findings.fix: No linter or formatter rule covers task composition. Either give `tasks.test` the `--coverage` flag so the thresholds in vitest.config.ts apply to the whole suite and drop `tasks.coverage` from the list, or keep `tasks.coverage` as a separate manual task and remove it from `check`.

findings.issue: `pr update` with a body and no title never runs at tool level. Coverage shows the cond-expr at 181 (`params.title !== undefined ? \`Title: ${params.title}\` : undefined`) with the alternate arm at count 0. The tool explicitly supports this shape - the guard at index.ts:178 accepts title OR body - and every tool-level test supplies a title (:254 supplies both, :267/:279/:288/:306/:320/:617 supply title only, :333 supplies neither). Editing only a PR description is a routine call, and the preview string built here is the only thing that tells the user, before a confirm-gated `gh pr edit`, exactly which field is about to change. I drove it against a stub gh: the dialog was `Pull request: current branch\nBody:\nnew desc` and gh received `pr edit --body new desc`, so the behaviour is correct, but inverting the arm (always emitting `Title: undefined`, or dropping the body line) would leave the suite fully green.
findings.fix: Add a tool-level test calling `{ operation: 'pr update', body: 'new desc' }` with a confirm spy that captures the dialog: assert the body contains `Body:\nnew desc`, does not contain `Title:`, and that `gh.callArgs()` equals `[['pr','edit','--body','new desc']]`. Add the declined variant asserting `gh.calls()` is empty, mirroring the existing declined tests.

findings.issue:
`const branch = branchResult.ok ? branchResult.stdout.trim() : ''` collapses two different conditions, and the `!branch` arm then reports a detached HEAD. v8 shows the alternate arm at count 0: no test makes `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` fail, so nothing pins what the tool says when git cannot report the branch. I drove it with a git stub that exits 3 for that one call: the tool returned `Committed:
...

Detached HEAD; check out a branch before pushing. The commit stays local.` on a repo that is emphatically on branch `main` with a normal commit on it. The push correctly stays local (it fails safe), but the message sends the user to a detached-HEAD fix for a git failure. A test written against the current string would fail on the wording, which is the point: this is a zero-coverage path that only reads as correct because nobody drove it.
findings.fix: Add a tool-level test with a `git` stub that execs the real binary except for `rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD`, which exits non-zero. Assert the result does NOT say `Detached HEAD` (it should name the git failure), and change line 76 so the detached message is gated on `branch === 'HEAD'` alone, with a separate `Could not determine the current branch (...)` text for the empty case.

findings.issue: The post-commit summary fallback `(params.message.split('\n')[0] ?? params.message)` never runs: coverage reports the right-hand side at count 0, so no test makes `git log -1 --format=%H%n%s` fail after a successful `git commit`. I drove it with a git stub that exits 3 for `log`: the tool returned `Committed:\nfeat: add b` using the message's own first line, which is the right behaviour, so this is a gap. It matters because the two sources can disagree - a commit-msg hook that rewrites the subject would make the fallback print something the user never committed, and no test distinguishes the two.
findings.fix: Add a test that stubs `git` to fail only for `log`, commits with a multi-line message, and asserts the result starts with `Committed:\nfeat: add b` and still reports the advisory hints.

findings.issue: Two error-detail chains in git-gh still inline what `detailOf` now centralises, and only their first arm is exercised. Coverage: line 107 (`human.stderr.trim() || human.stdout.trim() || '(no output from gh)'`) reports [1, 0, 0] and line 154 (`log.stderr.trim() || log.stdout.trim()`) reports [1, 0]. I drove both gaps and the behaviour is right - a logged-out gh whose message lands on stdout yields `gh is not authenticated:\nYou are not logged in (stdout only)`, and a silent failure yields `gh is not authenticated:\n(no output from gh)`. The prior round reported the same pattern across eight sites; three tools are now fixed via `detailOf` and these two inlines were left behind, so the remaining two are the stragglers.
findings.fix: Use `detailOf(human)` at line 107 and `detailOf(log)` at line 154. `detailOf` is already unit-tested for all three arms in tests/exec.test.ts, so this deletes the two untested chains instead of adding tests for them.

findings.issue: `if (pr.headRefName || pr.baseRefName) lines.push(`${pr.headRefName ?? '?'} -> ${pr.baseRefName ?? '?'}`)` never renders a `?`. Coverage reports the `baseRefName ?? '?'` arm at count 0, and the `formatPrView` fallback test (tests/git-gh.test.ts:886) only omits both refs, which skips the line entirely. gh omits `baseRefName` in practice for cross-fork PRs where the base is deleted, so this arm is reachable. I drove it: a PrView with `headRefName: 'feat'` and no base renders `feat -> ?` correctly.
findings.fix: Add one case to the existing `formatPrView` fallback test parsing `{"number":3,"title":"t","headRefName":"feat"}` and assert the rendered output contains `feat -> ?`.

findings.issue: All three operation dispatch switches (git-gh index.ts:192, git-worktree index.ts, git-commit's if/else) have no `default` case, so an operation outside the TypeBox union makes `execute` return `undefined` rather than a tool result. No test pins this. I drove it: `{ operation: 'nope' }` on the worktree tool returned `undefined` (my harness rendered `<<UNDEFINED RESULT: undefined>>`), not a text result. pi does validate tool arguments before `execute`, so the branch is currently unreachable, but every other failure mode in these three tools degrades to a text result and this one does not, and nothing would catch it if that validation changed or a new operation were added to the schema without a switch arm.
findings.fix: Add a `default:` arm to each switch returning `text(`Unknown operation: ${params.operation}.`)` and one test per tool calling an out-of-union operation and asserting the text. Alternatively add a test that asserts `execute` returns `undefined` today, so the behaviour is at least pinned rather than accidental.

findings.issue: Seven zero-count branch arms in the diff are unreachable defensive fallbacks that no test can cover, which is why branch coverage sits at 96.69% and not 100%: message.ts:25 `summary.trim().split(/\s+/)[0] ?? ''` (split always returns at least one string), message.ts:31 `subject.split('\n')[0] ?? ''`, message.ts:39/40 `match[1] ?? ''` and `match[2] ?? ''` (both groups are required by the regex), ghops.ts:132 `lines[0] ?? ''` (chunk is filtered non-empty before the split), git-commit/index.ts:107 `remotes[0] ?? ''` (guarded by `remotes.length === 1`), and exec.ts:59/60 `typeof stdout === 'string' ? stdout : ''` (the ternary exists only to narrow Buffer). Every one of them is forced by `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` or the `ExecFileOptions` overload, so the honest options are to delete the redundant half or to stop counting them.
findings.fix: Where the invariant is provable at the same line, drop the `?? ''` and let `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` stay satisfied by the preceding filter (ghops.ts:132 already has one). For exec.ts:59/60, use `String(stdout)` instead of the typeof ternary. If the rest stay, note them in a comment next to the perFile thresholds so a future reader does not chase them as gaps. A CI rule is not warranted here; these are compiler-driven, not style.

findings.issue: "// Arguments are NUL-terminated and each call ends with an empty NUL field, so // argument boundaries survive any byte an argument can contain." The protocol is entirely our own: the writer is `stubOnPath` at :133-135 (`printf '%s\000' "$@" ... printf '\000'`) in this same file. It also restates the loop immediately below (`for (const field of raw.split('\0'))` with the empty-field case pushing `current`), so the format is legible from the code without prose. Keep-list item 2 does not apply (own code, not a vendor wire format) and item 4 does not apply (`readCallArgs` is module-private, no external caller depends on the framing), so the justification is close to the mustKill bar. It survives only because the comment records the one thing the literals do not state: that the choice of NUL over newline exists so an argument containing a newline cannot forge a call boundary.
findings.fix: delete - if the anti-forgery rationale is wanted, the fix is to make the writer/reader contract structural rather than narrated: have `stubOnPath` write one JSON array per line (`printf '%s\n' "$@"` style is not enough, so push each argv vector through a length-prefixed or JSON-encoded frame) and drop `readCallArgs`' manual `split('\0')` loop for a `JSON.parse` per line, which removes the need for the note entirely.
